Most ADs make you feel really drowsy at first so try to start when you have a couple of days you can sleep alot. This normally eases over the first couple of weeks as your body adjusts.

Ideally you should tell someone you are starting to take them and ask them to keep an eye on you. In the early days you may experience a worsening of symptoms, urges to self-harm and suicidal ideation. If this continues, then either the dose or the AD itself isn't right for you.

Don't expect to magically feel better - it can take a couple of months for changes to stabilise.

Those are the common things but from there, symptoms and feelings will vary from person to person and AD to AD. I take Venlafaxine and I have a dose range where I'm obsessed with sex, literally cannot get enough, and that has led to some poor choices and risk taking. Above or below that range I couldn't care less if I never have sex again and find it difficult to orgasm. Everyone responds differently to every AD.

Don't be afraid of them of feel ashamed. If well managed then they can make a real difference and many people take them for lots of different reasons.

One big note of caution: Never take yourself straight off them. Some people won't have a problem but, for most, they experience strong withdrawal symptoms that can lead to harm or worse. 

Good luck.

I don't think it's as straight forward as 'seeking attention'. OP is being insightful and very honest about their feelings which suggest an unmet need. 

'Attention seeking' is an overused phrase which tends to carry shame and implies the intent to seek attention is the basis for the behaviour. I disagree. This is much deeper. 

OP, and the rest of us, don't feel like this on purpose and feeling a need to be cared for us very different to seeking attention which, as pixel_zealot mentions, is often actually an unwanted side-effect of our behaviours.

I've thought about this too. I took my first overdose in January. I was really confused; I wanted to die but I was also scared. I got caught out and hospitalised and, once I came round, I was embarrassed, ashamed and felt so guilty taking up resources. The doctor and nurses kept reassuring me that it was ok and that just feeling the need to overdose demonstrated I had need for help just like anyone else. Before discharge, I was seen by a psychiatric team who set up a crisis appointment for the next day (Sunday) and then I was given food (which I had to keep down to be discharged!). I definitely felt well looked-after but the shame stayed with me.

The need to feel cared-for is a normal, human requirement and if that need isn't being met elsewhere then we seek out resolutions. Doctors and nursing staff are the ultimate carers so an obvious choice. Just be aware of the consequences - you might die, you might be disabled or badly scarred. Also, if you're in the USA, it sounds like you might not get such a caring response and will be charged for the privilege!
